Ice Core Investigations
The precipitation which falls in the form of snow in areas of little or no melting provides a continuous record of the atmospheric history of that area. The ice contains entrapped foreign material that fell with or upon the snow. Ice cores provide a vertical profile of polar history and a unique opportunity to examine systematically the physical and chemical nature of an ice sheet as a function of depth. Stable and radioactive isotopes allow the establishment of age-depth relationships within the ice, and provide an opportunity to investigate the climatological trends and even significant meteorological disturbances that have affected the world's atmosphere. The ice cores will be examined for presence of heavy metals and other pollutants, and the variation of these through the vertical profile will also provide some understanding of their variation through time.
Detailed studies of the ice cores from the Ross Ice Shelf may provide some indication of possible interrelationships between climatic change and volcanic eruptions, cosmic showers, and variation in atmospheric circulation. If there were cyclic variations in the recent past such as have been suggested by Dansgaard and his co-workers in their Greenland investigations, the detailed record contained in the ice cores from the Ross Ice Shelf may provide additional information as to interhemispheric relationships of these cycles.
